laterality.verdict: bias survives drive equalisation: it is intrinsic to network dynamics, not input -> stop fixing the input, go to stage 2

ablate.verdict: readout is knife-edge: perturbing 1.0% of neurons already moves difference_hz by sd 2.94 Hz against a 2 Hz threshold, and spread reaches 14x the threshold under ablation. The label is held by a standing bias, not by the signal -> the decoder needs to INTEGRATE over the window, not just widen to more cells

reinforce.verdict: reinforcement carries signal: presence moves the memory 11.6% (relative L1) against a 3,401-edge endogenous baseline, timing moves it 2.6%. Presence dominates timing 4.6x -- the rule responds mostly to HOW MUCH dopamine arrived, not WHEN. GA is unblocked, but what it can select on is dose, not credit assignment

separation.verdict: the chart reaches the mushroom body with at most 0.07% of Kenyon cells in EVERY rendering, so this comparison is not measuring the picture. The visual pathway does not deliver a code at the shipped excitation/inhibition ratio; renderings were last told apart at ratio 1.0, where the filled area removed all ten collisions the polyline caused. Input separation still differs -- 4.19% of receptors for 'polyline' against 17.73% filled -- but nothing downstream of the retina is using it

sparseness.verdict: no declared free parameter reaches the 1%-15% band: across the whole kc_rest x apl_gain grid the median Kenyon activity goes 0.05% to 18.52% without stopping in between, and over all 196 observations only 6% land inside the band against 84% near-silent and 10% above 20%. The population is bistable, so sparseness cannot be set by gain alone (strongest levers: adaptation_jump 0.10%-33.12%, kc_rest 0.05%-18.52%). Separately: 17 of 30 grid points produce more than one distinct decision and 23 of 196 observations propose SELL, where every input manipulation tested before produced none -- but the widest SELL margin is 4 spikes past the threshold against 6 for BUY, so this is the readout coming off its rail, not the fly changing its mind

olfaction.verdict: the odour reaches the mushroom body -- 0/28 identical glomerular codes and 0/28 identical Kenyon codes against 6/28 for the chart -- but the receptor population is itself a step: it emits no spike at all up to current 5 and saturates the Kenyon population immediately above it. At the best of 25 current x APL-gain points (current 30, APL x2) Kenyon activity is 7.46%-8.66% with 8/8 states in the 1%-15% band and mean overlap 0.77. No point in the grid is both sparse and separable (overlap at or below 0.5 with all 8 states in band), so the odour channel removes the collisions without removing the bistability -- the population still has two states and the input only chooses between them

kc_input.verdict: summed excitatory input onto a Kenyon cell spans 26.4 to 509.9 in the reconstruction, a factor of 19. Equalising it lowers the overlap at 0 of 3 gains but never far enough to be usable (sparse in all 8 states with overlap at or below 0.5): APL x1: overlap 0.88 -> 0.89, in band 0->0; APL x2: overlap 0.76 -> 0.76, in band 8->8; APL x4: overlap 0.53 -> 0.60, in band 0->0. The Kenyon population is not selecting on which glomeruli are active, so the loudest-cell hypothesis does not by itself explain the shared code

odor_tuning.verdict: sharpening the tuning curve takes the input overlap from 0.44 to 0.19 and the Kenyon overlap from 0.76 to 0.79, a transfer of -0.12 (sigma 0.9/floor 0.1: 17.2 glomeruli, input overlap 0.44, Kenyon overlap 0.76, in band 8; sigma 0.6/floor 0.3: 8.5 glomeruli, input overlap 0.34, Kenyon overlap 0.78, in band 8; sigma 0.5/floor 0.5: 7.2 glomeruli, input overlap 0.34, Kenyon overlap 0.79, in band 8; sigma 0.3/floor 0.3: 4.9 glomeruli, input overlap 0.19, Kenyon overlap 0.79, in band 8). No width is both sparse in every state and below 0.5 overlap. A transfer well under 1 means the shared Kenyon code is made in the mushroom body, not inherited from the receptors, so sharpening the input further is the wrong lever

pathway.verdict: overlap along the path: glomerular code 0.44 -> receptors 0.61 -> hop1 0.98 -> hop2 0.87 -> kenyon 0.76. The convergence happens at receptors -> hop1, which adds +0.37 on its own. That synapse is where the market signal stops being a difference between states, and it is the only place worth changing

inhibition.verdict: scaling all 9,813,608 inhibitory edges (38% of the graph): x1: antennal lobe 0.98, Kenyon 0.88, in band 0; x1.5: antennal lobe 0.93, Kenyon 0.64, in band 8; x1.6: antennal lobe 0.92, Kenyon 0.60, in band 8; x1.7: antennal lobe 0.92, Kenyon 0.57, in band 8; x1.8: antennal lobe 0.92, Kenyon 0.52, in band 8; x1.9: antennal lobe 0.91, Kenyon 0.50, in band 8; x2: antennal lobe 0.90, Kenyon 0.49, in band 5; x2.5: antennal lobe 0.87, Kenyon 0.32, in band 0; x3: antennal lobe 0.84, Kenyon 0.32, in band 0. x1.9 gives a Kenyon code that is sparse in every state and separable at overlap 0.50, against 0.88 as reconstructed

pulse.verdict: the same amplitude reaches 15 reward cells and 2 aversive ones, so per-cell drive is unequal: reward/aversive ratio by current -- 20: 14.7x; 30: 12.4x; 40: 1.5x; 60: 1.0x; 80: 1.0x; 120: 1.0x. At the shipped 20 the aversive compartment gets 1.0 spikes per cell against 14.7 for reward. 40 is the smallest amplitude that drives both within 2x (32.2 against 21.0 spikes per cell)

decoder.verdict: signal-to-noise, spread across eight market states over the standard deviation under 5% ablation: descending 0.66; descending_and_motor 0.64; dnp20_shipped 0.43. Every candidate is below 1, so for all of them the market moves the readout less than silencing unrelated neurons does. Widening the readout does not fix that, and a decoder is not the missing piece yet
